understanding.bridge: What you are living with is what the texts call fear of what might happen, and that is where this week begins.
understanding.week_thesis: Seven days from a mind that will not rest to a mind that can hold the days without breaking, starting with one hour that is not about work.

week_beats.hook: You recognise the terror and the sleeplessness as a state, not a character flaw.
week_beats.steady: You hold that what is real in you cannot be taken by a rating or a visa.
week_beats.act: You try one hour before bed that is not about work, and one honest conversation with your wife about the fear.
week_beats.story: A man who had everything to lose and a wife who had given up her own life for it shows you that rest is not surrender.

understanding.core_struggle: A husband who cannot sleep because a bad rating in days means losing his visa and leaving his wife, who gave up her career, behind.
understanding.mirror: You check the messages at 2am, and the weekend becomes just another workday.
understanding.insight: Most of what you fear hasn't happened. Your mind keeps living it in advance, again and again.

verse.speaker: Arjuna
verse.setting: Arjuna, seeing his own family in the enemy ranks, collapses in grief before the battle.
verse.sanskrit: सीदन्ति मम गात्राणि मुखं च परिशुष्यति । वेपथुश्च शरीरे मे रोमहर्षश्च जायते ॥ गाण्डीवं स्रंसते हस्तात्त्वक्चैव परिदह्यते । न च शक्नोम्यवस्थातुं भ्रमतीव च मे मनः ॥
verse.line: Shaking limbs, a dry mouth, a racing body: the Gita opens with a panic attack, not a hero.
verse.translation: My limbs give way, my mouth is parched, my body trembles and my hair stands on end.
verse.why: Even the strongest people freeze; the Gita begins with a breakdown, not a hero.
verse.misuse: Not a dismissal of anxiety; it shows that even the strong feel it, and the teaching starts there.

prasang.title: Overcome by delusion, Arjuna speaks in fear, love and grief
prasang.summary: Seeing his kin ready to die, Arjuna trembles, his bow slips, and he argues that no victory is worth killing family. He sits down in the chariot and refuses to fight.
prasang.story_hook: The greatest archer of his age stood between two armies, and his hands began to shake.
prasang.lesson: Even the strongest people freeze; the Gita begins with a breakdown, not a hero.

verse.meaning: Arjuna stands in his chariot between two armies, and sees his own kin ready to kill one another. His body shakes, his mouth goes dry, his hair stands on end. The Gita opens with a man freezing, not a hero stepping forward. It says that even the strongest can collapse, and the teaching begins inside that collapse. The verse proposes what is already happening: the body is telling the truth about the fear, and it is allowed to feel it.
verse.for_you: Your body knows what your mind is trying to outrun. That dry mouth and the trembling limbs are not a failure. They are the truth of what is happening. Let them be there without fighting them.

verse.speaker: Bhasa
verse.setting: Two childhood friends meet again in old age; one admits he never found peace.
verse.sanskrit: उह्यमानमनन्तेषु चेतः कार्यमहोर्मिषु । क्षणमेति न विश्रान्तिं चिन्ताताण्डविताशयम् ॥ इदं कृतं करोमीदं करिष्यामीदमित्यलम् । कलनाजालवलिता मूर्च्छिता मतिपक्षिणी ॥
verse.line: 'Done this, doing this, must do that.' Caught in endless lists, the mind never gets a moment's rest.
verse.translation: Carried along on endless great waves of tasks, the mind never gets a moment's rest; its depths dance with worry. 'This I've done, this I'm doing, this I'll do': so the bird of the mind, tangled in a net of reckonings, faints.
verse.why: Years of hard effort without inner understanding can leave you exactly where you started.

prasang.title: Two old friends meet again and admit they never found peace
prasang.summary: Bhasa and Vilasa grow up inseparable in a forest hermitage. After their fathers die they drift apart and spend long lonely years in hard austerities. When they meet again as old men, one asks if the other is well; he answers honestly that there is no wellness while the mind keeps spinning through endless tasks and worries.
prasang.story_hook: They had been inseparable as boys, and when they met again they were old men with nothing to show.
prasang.lesson: Years of hard effort without inner understanding can leave you exactly where you started.

verse.meaning: Bhasa and Vilasa are old men now. They grew up together in a forest hermitage, then spent decades apart in lonely, hard austerities. When they meet again, Bhasa asks how he is. Vilasa answers honestly that there is no wellness while the mind keeps spinning through endless tasks and worries. He says the mind is carried along on great waves of tasks, never resting. It dances with worry, tangled in a net of reckonings: what was done, what is being done, what must be done next.
verse.for_you: Your mind is caught in that same net of reckonings right now. It is racing through the work messages at two in the morning, rehearsing the bad rating, the visa, the leaving. The worry is real, but the mind is not resting. It is fainting under the weight of what has not happened yet.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on how to act without being chained to results.
verse.sanskrit: कर्मण्येवाधिकारस्ते मा फलेषु कदाचन । मा कर्मफलहेतुर्भूर्मा ते सङ्गोऽस्त्वकर्मणि ॥
verse.line: Your work is yours to do; the results are not yours to hold. Don't let that make you stop.
verse.translation: Your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits. Do not let the fruit be your motive, and do not cling to doing nothing.
verse.why: Do the work fully; let go of owning the result.
verse.misuse: This is not 'don't care about results' or 'don't plan'. Care, plan and aim well; just don't let the outcome own you.

prasang.title: The calm of the wise
prasang.summary: In a hundred verses Ashtavakra paints the inner peace of the wise: calm while busy, unmoved by gain or loss, praise or blame, at ease whether in the city or the forest. The restless, by contrast, chase peace and never find it.
prasang.lesson: Calm isn't found by chasing it or changing places; it is how you hold ordinary life.

verse.meaning: In the long closing chapter of the Ashtavakra Gita, Ashtavakra speaks to Janaka about the calm of the wise. He says that a steady mind does not beg for gain or grieve over loss. It stays cool, filled as if with nectar, no matter what happens in the world outside. This calm is not found by chasing it or changing places. It is how you hold ordinary life.
verse.for_you: Your mind is racing because it is begging for a good rating and grieving the bad one. The calm you need is not in the phone. It is in how you hold this hour. Let the rating be what it is. Let your mind be what it is. Do not beg for a different outcome.

prasang.title: How a free person lives
prasang.summary: Ribhu describes how a free person lives among others: letting go of what is lost, taking up what comes, doing the work at hand, speaking gently, busy outside and calm inside, and treating the whole world as family.
prasang.lesson: Live fully in the world while staying unhurried inside.

verse.meaning: Ribhu tells Nidagha how a free person lives. He is busy on the outside, but inside he is still. story.title: King Janaka overhears the sages and keeps ruling, with a free mind
story.story_hook: One spring morning, a king out for a walk overheard a song that he could not stop thinking about.
story.summary: Walking in his spring garden, King Janaka overhears hidden sages singing about the self. Shaken, he climbs to his palace roof and questions everything he has lived for. When his doorkeeper calls him to the day's work, he decides not to run away: he gets up and does his duties, but with a mind that no longer clutches.

script: Your body is awake right now. The phone is still in your hand, and your mind is running through the same thoughts it has run before. You are carrying the weight of a visa that might not come through, and your chest feels tight. You are not wrong to feel this.
Arjuna stands in his chariot between two armies, and sees his own kin ready to kill one another. His body shakes, his mouth goes dry, his hair stands on end. Arjuna said:
सीदन्ति मम गात्राणि मुखं च परिशुष्यति, वेपथुश्च शरीरे मे रोमहर्षश्च जायते. गाण्डीवं स्रंसते हस्तात्त्वक्चैव परिदह्यते, न च शक्नोम्यवस्थातुं भ्रमतीव च मे मनः.
In plain words: Shaking limbs, a dry mouth, a racing body: the Gita opens with a panic attack, not a hero.

The verse tells us that the body knows the truth before the mind can speak it. Your limbs are shaking and your mouth is dry because your body is already in the future you fear. This is not a sign that you are weak. It is a sign that you are human. The teaching begins right here, in the collapse, not after it. The body is telling the truth about the fear, and it is allowed to feel it.

Right now, you are holding the phone and checking messages. Let your hand rest on the table for ten seconds and feel the surface beneath it. Let your body be dry and trembling without trying to fix it. You do not need to solve the visa tonight. You only need to let your body be where it is.
What if the trembling and the dry mouth are just your body telling the truth?

depth.points: Arjuna is a warrior, yet his body betrays him. The Gita shows that panic is not a sign of weakness, but the honest starting point of the teaching. What you feel is the truth of what is happening, not a failure to be fixed.
depth.practice: Set a timer for five minutes and place your phone out of reach. Just sit with the dry mouth and the trembling, and let them be there without trying to fix them.
depth.question: What if you let your body finish what your mind keeps starting?
